topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A seller removes a built-in wall oven before closing, arguing it was a personal appliance. The buyer objects, saying it was part of the price. Under the common-law test for fixtures, which factor is generally given the MOST weight by courts?
choice_a: The intention of the party who installed the item, as shown by objective circumstances
choice_b: The dollar amount the item originally cost
choice_c: Whether the item is plugged in or hardwired
choice_d: The color and style of the item relative to the rest of the kitchen
explanation: Courts applying the fixture test weigh method of annexation, adaptation to the property's use, and the relationship between the parties, but the objective intention of the annexor (inferred from how firmly and permanently the item is attached and used) is treated as the controlling factor. A built-in oven wired into cabinetry strongly signals intent to make it a permanent part of the real property, which is why it passes with the sale absent a contrary agreement.
source_note: Universal common-law fixture doctrine (annexation/adaptation/intention test); Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Real Property Elements.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A retail tenant installs commercial display shelving and a walk-in cooler in a leased space to run her business. When the lease ends, she wants to remove them. These items are best classified as:
choice_a: Real property that automatically transfers to the landlord
choice_b: Trade fixtures, which the tenant may remove before the lease expires
choice_c: Emblements
choice_d: Appurtenances that run with the land
explanation: Trade fixtures are items a commercial tenant installs to conduct business and are treated as the tenant's personal property despite being attached to the premises. The tenant has the right to remove them, provided removal occurs before the lease term ends and the tenant repairs any damage caused by removal.
source_note: Common-law trade fixture doctrine, an exception to the general fixture rule; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A deed conveys a parcel of land "together with all appurtenances thereto." An appurtenance is best described as:
choice_a: A movable item of personal property left behind by the seller
choice_b: A structure that violates the setback line
choice_c: A right or interest that is attached to and passes with the land, such as an easement
choice_d: A tax lien recorded against the property
explanation: An appurtenance is a right, privilege, or improvement that belongs to and passes with the land even though it is not a physical part of it, such as an easement, water right, or air right. Appurtenant rights transfer automatically with a conveyance of the land unless expressly reserved or excluded.
source_note: Standard real property terminology; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Real Property Elements.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A farm is sold in September, after the seller/tenant farmer has already planted a soybean crop that will not be harvested until November. Absent a contrary agreement, who has the right to the growing annual crop?
choice_a: The buyer, because crops pass automatically with title to the land
choice_b: The county extension office, until the dispute is resolved
choice_c: Whoever holds the mineral rights
choice_d: The seller/tenant, under the doctrine of emblements
explanation: Emblements (fructus industriales) are annually cultivated crops produced by labor, and the common-law doctrine of emblements allows the party who planted and cultivated the crop to return and harvest it even after their interest in the land has ended, unless the parties' contract provides otherwise.
source_note: Common-law doctrine of emblements distinguishing fructus industriales from fructus naturales; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: The full "bundle of legal rights" associated with real property ownership includes all of the following EXCEPT:
choice_a: The right to violate recorded zoning ordinances if the owner disagrees with them
choice_b: The right to possess
choice_c: The right to control use within the law
choice_d: The right to exclude others
explanation: The bundle of rights includes the rights to possess, use and control, enjoy, exclude, and dispose of property. It does not include a right to disregard valid governmental regulation such as zoning; those rights are always held subject to the public police power, taxation, eminent domain, and escheat.
source_note: Standard bundle-of-rights theory of ownership; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A parcel borders a non-navigable stream. The owner's rights to reasonable use of the water bordering and crossing the land, subject to the rights of other riparian owners, are known as:
choice_a: Littoral rights
choice_b: Riparian rights
choice_c: Avulsion rights
choice_d: Doctrine of prior appropriation
explanation: Riparian rights belong to owners of land bordering a flowing waterway such as a river or stream and generally include reasonable use of the water. Littoral rights, by contrast, apply to land bordering static bodies of water such as lakes, seas, or oceans.
source_note: Standard water-rights terminology distinguishing riparian from littoral rights; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A homeowner sells a lot with several mature oak trees still standing. Because these perennial trees were not planted as part of an annual farming operation, the law classifies them as:
choice_a: Fructus industriales, and they transfer separately as personal property
choice_b: Trade fixtures
choice_c: Fructus naturales, part of the real property that transfers automatically with the land
choice_d: Emblements reserved to the seller
explanation: Naturally occurring perennial vegetation such as trees, grasses, and shrubs (fructus naturales) is considered real property and passes automatically with a conveyance of the land, unlike annually cultivated crops (fructus industriales/emblements), which can be treated as personal property under certain circumstances.
source_note: Common-law distinction between fructus naturales and fructus industriales; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A landowner sells the subsurface mineral rights to a mining company while retaining the surface for residential use. This transaction demonstrates that real property rights are:
choice_a: Indivisible and must always be conveyed as a single unit
choice_b: Automatically extinguished once mineral rights are sold
choice_c: Void because Arkansas prohibits split estates
choice_d: Divisible, since air, surface, and subsurface rights can be severed and conveyed separately
explanation: Real property consists of the surface, the airspace above it, and the subsurface below it, and these components can be severed and owned or conveyed separately, creating a "split estate." Mineral rights, air rights, and surface rights are commonly separated through deeds or reservations.
source_note: Standard surface/subsurface/air rights severability doctrine; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Which estate in land grants the owner the maximum bundle of rights, of potentially infinite duration, with no conditions attached to its continuation?
choice_a: Fee simple absolute
choice_b: Life estate
choice_c: Estate for years
choice_d: Tenancy at sufferance
explanation: Fee simple absolute is the highest and most complete form of ownership recognized in real property law. It is of potentially infinite duration, freely inheritable, and unconditional, meaning the owner holds every right in the bundle without restriction or a triggering condition.
source_note: Foundational freehold estate doctrine; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Forms of Ownership.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A deed states, "To the City, so long as the land is used as a public park." If the city ever stops using the land as a park, title:
choice_a: Remains with the city permanently regardless of use
choice_b: Automatically reverts to the grantor or the grantor's heirs by operation of law
choice_c: Passes to whoever is currently renting the park facilities
choice_d: Requires the grantor to file a quiet title lawsuit before any interest changes hands
explanation: Language such as "so long as" creates a fee simple determinable. This estate automatically ends and title reverts to the grantor (or the grantor's heirs) the instant the stated condition is violated, without need for any further action such as a lawsuit or re-entry.
source_note: Defeasible fee doctrine (fee simple determinable vs. condition subsequent); Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A deed states, "To the City, but if the land is ever used for anything other than a public park, the grantor may re-enter and retake the property." This creates which estate?
choice_a: Fee simple determinable
choice_b: A life estate pur autre vie
choice_c: Fee simple subject to a condition subsequent
choice_d: A periodic tenancy
explanation: Language granting a "right of re-entry" or "power of termination" upon breach of a stated condition creates a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent. Unlike a fee simple determinable, title does not revert automatically; the grantor must take affirmative action to exercise the right of re-entry.
source_note: Defeasible fee doctrine; distinguishes automatic reversion from a grantor's optional right of re-entry; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A grandmother conveys her home "to my son for the life of my granddaughter." This unusual form of life estate, measured by the life of someone other than the holder, is called:
choice_a: A remainder interest
choice_b: A reversionary fee
choice_c: A leasehold estate
choice_d: A life estate pur autre vie
explanation: A life estate pur autre vie ("for the life of another") is measured by the lifespan of a person other than the life tenant. Here, the son holds the life estate, but its duration is tied to the granddaughter's life, not his own.
source_note: Life estate variations; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Forms of Ownership.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A life tenant in possession has a legal duty to the remainderman or reversioner to:
choice_a: Avoid committing waste, and generally maintain the property and pay ordinary taxes and carrying costs
choice_b: Sell the property before the life estate ends
choice_c: Convert the life estate into a fee simple within five years
choice_d: Obtain the remainderman's written consent before living in the home
explanation: A life tenant may use and enjoy the property but must not commit waste — voluntary (affirmative damage), permissive (neglect), or ameliorative (unauthorized changes, even if they increase value) — that would harm the interest of the remainderman or reversioner. The life tenant is also generally responsible for ordinary upkeep, insurance, and property taxes during the life estate.
source_note: Life tenant duties and the doctrine of waste; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A tenant signs a written lease for a fixed term of exactly 12 months beginning June 1. This creates which type of leasehold estate?
choice_a: Periodic tenancy
choice_b: Estate (tenancy) for years
choice_c: Tenancy at will
choice_d: Tenancy at sufferance
explanation: An estate for years (or tenancy for years) has a definite, agreed-upon beginning and ending date, regardless of its actual length — even a one-month lease qualifies if the term is fixed. It terminates automatically at the end of the stated term without notice being required.
source_note: Standard leasehold estate classification; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Forms of Ownership.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A tenant's lease has expired, but she continues occupying the unit without the landlord's consent and without paying rent. Her legal status is best described as:
choice_a: Periodic tenancy
choice_b: Estate for years
choice_c: Tenancy at sufferance
choice_d: Life estate
explanation: A tenancy at sufferance arises when a tenant who lawfully took possession remains in the property after the right to possession has ended, without the landlord's consent. It is the lowest form of leasehold interest, essentially a holdover, and the landlord may treat the occupant as a trespasser or elect to create a new periodic tenancy.
source_note: Standard leasehold classification (holdover tenancy); Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Three unrelated investors want to hold title so that when one dies, that investor's share passes automatically to the surviving co-owners rather than to the deceased investor's heirs. Which form of co-ownership accomplishes this?
choice_a: Tenancy in common
choice_b: Tenancy by the entirety
choice_c: Community property
choice_d: Joint tenancy with right of survivorship
explanation: Joint tenancy includes the right of survivorship, meaning a deceased joint tenant's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s) by operation of law, bypassing probate and the deceased owner's will. Traditional joint tenancy requires the four unities of time, title, interest, and possession.
source_note: Standard concurrent ownership doctrine; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Forms of Ownership.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Two joint tenants own a property together. One joint tenant sells her interest to a third party without the other's consent. What is the effect on title?
choice_a: The joint tenancy is severed as to that share; the buyer and the remaining original owner now hold as tenants in common
choice_b: The sale is void because joint tenancy interests cannot be conveyed without unanimous consent
choice_c: The right of survivorship remains fully intact for all parties
choice_d: The remaining original joint tenant automatically acquires the entire property
explanation: A joint tenant can unilaterally convey her interest during her lifetime, but doing so destroys the unity of time and/or title as to that share, severing the joint tenancy. The new owner takes as a tenant in common with the remaining original owner, and the right of survivorship no longer applies to that severed share.
source_note: Joint tenancy severance doctrine (four unities); Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Two siblings inherit a property together, each owning a 50% undivided interest, with no right of survivorship. Each can sell, mortgage, or will their share independently. This describes:
choice_a: Joint tenancy
choice_b: Tenancy in common
choice_c: Tenancy by the entirety
choice_d: Severalty ownership
explanation: Tenancy in common allows two or more owners to hold undivided interests in a property, which may be unequal in size, without a right of survivorship. Each co-tenant can freely transfer, mortgage, or devise their individual interest by will without the consent of the other co-tenants.
source_note: Standard concurrent ownership doctrine; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Forms of Ownership.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A married couple purchases a home together in Arkansas and takes title as tenants by the entirety. What is a key legal consequence of this form of ownership?
choice_a: Either spouse may unilaterally convey or mortgage the entire property without the other's signature
choice_b: The property can be reached by a creditor of only one spouse to satisfy that spouse's individual debt
choice_c: Neither spouse can convey their interest alone, and the property generally is not subject to the claims of one spouse's individual creditors
choice_d: The tenancy is treated identically to a plain tenancy in common with no survivorship feature
explanation: Arkansas recognizes tenancy by the entirety as a special form of concurrent ownership available only to married couples. Both spouses are treated as owning the whole property together; neither may unilaterally convey or encumber the property, and because each spouse is not deemed to own a separable individual share, the property generally cannot be reached by the individual creditors of only one spouse. It also carries a right of survivorship.
source_note: Arkansas recognizes tenancy by the entirety for married couples, a distinct form of concurrent ownership with creditor-protection and unanimous-conveyance features; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Forms of Ownership.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: An out-of-state buyer relocating to Arkansas asks her agent whether Arkansas is a "community property" state, where property acquired during marriage is automatically owned 50/50 by both spouses. The agent should explain that:
choice_a: Arkansas is a community property state, identical to Texas or California
choice_b: Arkansas abolished all forms of marital property rights in real estate
choice_c: Community property only applies to personal property, never real property, in every state
choice_d: Arkansas is a common-law property state; ownership generally depends on how title is actually taken, such as tenancy by the entirety, joint tenancy, or tenancy in common
explanation: Arkansas is a common-law (separate property) state, not a community property state. Ownership of real property acquired during a marriage is determined by how title is taken (for example, tenancy by the entirety, joint tenancy, or tenancy in common), rather than an automatic 50/50 community property presumption used in community property states.
source_note: Arkansas is a common-law property state, not a community property state; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: In a condominium, an individual owner's interest typically consists of:
choice_a: Fee simple ownership of the unit's airspace combined with a tenancy-in-common interest, shared with other owners, in the common elements
choice_b: A leasehold interest in the unit only, with no ownership rights
choice_c: A life estate in the unit that terminates when the owner sells any other property
choice_d: Sole ownership of the entire building, including all other units
explanation: Condominium ownership typically combines fee simple title to the airspace within an individual unit with an undivided tenancy-in-common interest, shared proportionally with all other unit owners, in the building's common elements such as hallways, roofs, and grounds.
source_note: Standard condominium ownership structure; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Forms of Ownership.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A metes-and-bounds legal description of a parcel must always:
choice_a: Reference a recorded subdivision plat map
choice_b: Begin and end at the same identifiable point of beginning, so the boundary closes
choice_c: Reference a township and range from a principal meridian
choice_d: State the total acreage rounded to the nearest whole number
explanation: A metes-and-bounds description traces a parcel's boundary using compass directions (bearings) and distances (metes) starting from an identifiable point of beginning (POB) and proceeding around the perimeter until it returns to that same point, closing the boundary. If the description does not mathematically close, it is legally defective.
source_note: Standard metes-and-bounds description mechanics; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Legal Descriptions.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Arkansas land was originally surveyed and is still described under the U.S. Public Land Survey System (government/rectangular survey system). Under this system, a standard "township" is:
choice_a: A parcel exactly one acre in size
choice_b: A subdivision equal to one-quarter of a section
choice_c: A square measuring six miles by six miles, containing 36 sections
choice_d: A boundary drawn using metes and bounds only
explanation: Under the government (rectangular) survey system used across much of Arkansas, a township is a six-mile-by-six-mile square (36 square miles) subdivided into 36 numbered sections, each one square mile (640 acres). Townships are located relative to a principal meridian (a north-south reference line) and a base line (an east-west reference line).
source_note: U.S. Public Land Survey System (government survey), used in Arkansas; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Legal Descriptions.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Under the government survey system, one section of land contains 640 acres. How many acres are in the NE 1/4 of the NW 1/4 of a section?
choice_a: 10 acres
choice_b: 20 acres
choice_c: 160 acres
choice_d: 40 acres
explanation: A quarter section is 640 ÷ 4 = 160 acres. A quarter of that quarter (the NE 1/4 of the NW 1/4) is 160 ÷ 4 = 40 acres. This step-by-step fractional method is standard for calculating acreage from a government survey legal description.
source_note: Government survey acreage calculation; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Legal Descriptions.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A legal description reads: "Lot 14, Block 3, Sunset Ridge Addition, as recorded in Plat Book 22, Page 47." This is an example of which type of legal description?
choice_a: Lot-and-block (recorded plat) description
choice_b: Metes and bounds
choice_c: Government (rectangular) survey
choice_d: Informal street address description
explanation: The lot-and-block system identifies a specific parcel by referencing its lot and block number as shown on a recorded subdivision plat map, which itself contains the detailed metes-and-bounds or survey data. This method is the most common way developers describe individual lots within a platted subdivision.
source_note: Lot-and-block (recorded plat) description method; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Legal Descriptions.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Parcel A and Parcel B are adjoining lots. Parcel A's owner has a recorded right to cross a strip of Parcel B to reach the public road. If Parcel B is sold to a new owner, that right of crossing:
choice_a: Terminates automatically upon sale of Parcel B
choice_b: Continues to burden Parcel B and benefit Parcel A, because an easement appurtenant runs with the land
choice_c: Must be repurchased by Parcel A's owner from the new owner of Parcel B
choice_d: Converts into a license that either party may revoke at will
explanation: An easement appurtenant involves a dominant estate (Parcel A, which benefits) and a servient estate (Parcel B, which is burdened). Because it "runs with the land," it automatically transfers with both parcels regardless of changes in ownership, unless properly extinguished (for example, by release, merger, or abandonment).
source_note: Easement appurtenant doctrine (dominant/servient estate); Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Legal Descriptions/Easements.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A utility company holds a recorded right to install and maintain power lines across a homeowner's property, but the utility does not own any adjoining land that benefits from the right. This is an example of:
choice_a: An easement appurtenant
choice_b: A prescriptive easement
choice_c: An easement in gross
choice_d: An encroachment
explanation: An easement in gross benefits a specific person or entity rather than a neighboring parcel of land — there is a servient estate but no dominant estate. Commercial easements in gross, such as those held by utility companies, are typically assignable and transferable even without an accompanying parcel of land.
source_note: Easement in gross doctrine, contrasted with easement appurtenant; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A neighbor has openly used a gravel driveway crossing a corner of an adjoining owner's land, without permission, continuously and visibly, for the entire statutory period required by state law. This conduct may give rise to which right?
choice_a: Fee simple title to the entire adjoining lot by adverse possession
choice_b: An automatic termination of the adjoining owner's easement in gross
choice_c: A leasehold estate for years
choice_d: An easement by prescription, granting a continuing right to use that portion of land
explanation: A prescriptive easement arises when someone uses another's land in a manner that is open, notorious, continuous, and adverse (without permission) for the period required by the applicable statute of limitations. Unlike adverse possession, a prescriptive easement grants only a right to use the land for a specific purpose, not full ownership of the underlying fee.
source_note: Easement by prescription doctrine, distinguished from adverse possession; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A single owner sells the rear portion of a large lot to a buyer, leaving the buyer's new parcel with no direct access to any public road. Which type of easement may a court impose to remedy this situation?
choice_a: Easement by necessity
choice_b: Easement in gross
choice_c: Negative easement
choice_d: License
explanation: An easement by necessity is implied when a common grantor's division of land leaves one resulting parcel landlocked with no legal access to a public road. Courts will imply this easement across the remaining land of the common grantor (or successor) because access is considered a fundamental necessity, not merely a convenience.
source_note: Easement by necessity doctrine, arising from severance by a common grantor; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A homeowner gives a neighbor oral permission to walk across her backyard to reach a fishing pond, revocable at any time. This permission is best classified as:
choice_a: An easement appurtenant
choice_b: A license
choice_c: An easement in gross that binds future owners
choice_d: A prescriptive easement
explanation: A license is a personal, revocable permission to use another's land for a specific purpose. Unlike an easement, a license is not an interest in land, does not run with the land, and can typically be revoked by the licensor at will and does not survive a transfer of the property.
source_note: License vs. easement distinction; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A new survey reveals that a neighbor's garage was built two feet over the property line onto the adjoining lot. This physical intrusion is called:
choice_a: An easement by necessity
choice_b: A restrictive covenant violation
choice_c: An encroachment
choice_d: A variance
explanation: An encroachment occurs when a structure, fence, driveway, or other improvement unlawfully extends onto a neighboring owner's property. Encroachments are typically discovered through a boundary survey and can be resolved by removal, a boundary line agreement, or a negotiated easement allowing the encroachment to remain.
source_note: Standard encroachment doctrine; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Legal Descriptions/Easements.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Adjoining owners discover a discrepancy between their deeds and the actual fence line that has existed for decades. To resolve the dispute without going to court, they can sign and record a document establishing the fence as the true boundary. This tool is called:
choice_a: A quitclaim of easement in gross
choice_b: A certificate of title
choice_c: A deed restriction
choice_d: A boundary line agreement
explanation: A boundary line agreement is a recorded document in which adjoining owners mutually agree on the location of their shared boundary, often used to resolve uncertainty or a long-standing discrepancy between a fence line and the record legal description, avoiding costly litigation.
source_note: Standard boundary dispute resolution tool; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Two adjacent commercial buildings share a single wall straddling the property line, with each owner having reciprocal rights to use and maintain it. This shared structure is an example of:
choice_a: A party wall subject to a party wall easement
choice_b: A trade fixture
choice_c: An easement by prescription
choice_d: A leasehold improvement
explanation: A party wall sits on or straddles the boundary line between two properties and is used to support structures on both sides. Party walls typically carry mutual (reciprocal) easement rights and obligations, requiring both owners to share in maintenance and give consent before making certain modifications.
source_note: Party wall doctrine, a specialized form of shared easement; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes riparian rights from littoral rights?
choice_a: Littoral rights apply only to subsurface mineral rights
choice_b: Riparian rights apply to owners bordering flowing waterways like rivers and streams; littoral rights apply to owners bordering static bodies of water like lakes and oceans
choice_c: Riparian and littoral rights are simply two different names for the same identical right
choice_d: Littoral rights apply to flowing waterways and riparian rights apply to static bodies of water
explanation: Riparian rights belong to owners of land adjoining rivers, streams, and other flowing watercourses. Littoral rights belong to owners of land adjoining static or standing bodies of water such as lakes, seas, and oceans. Both give varying rights of reasonable use, access, and (in some jurisdictions) accretion.
source_note: Standard water-rights terminology; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: For a deed to be legally valid, its legal description of the property must be:
choice_a: Written exclusively in the government survey format
choice_b: Limited to the mailing address only
choice_c: Sufficiently definite and certain that the property can be located and identified with reasonable accuracy
choice_d: Approved in advance by the county zoning board
explanation: A valid legal description must identify the property with enough certainty that a surveyor could locate its exact boundaries. A street address alone is generally not considered a sufficient legal description for a deed because it can change or be ambiguous, whereas metes-and-bounds, government survey, and lot-and-block descriptions are all acceptable methods when properly drafted.
source_note: General requirement that a legal description be definite enough to identify the property; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A commercial lender financing a large tract requires an ALTA/NSPS land title survey before closing. The primary purpose of this type of survey is to:
choice_a: Determine the property's current market value
choice_b: Replace the need for a title search entirely
choice_c: Establish the zoning classification of the parcel
choice_d: Identify boundary lines, improvements, easements, and encroachments to standards acceptable for title insurance purposes
explanation: An ALTA/NSPS survey is a detailed boundary and improvement survey prepared to a national standard used in commercial transactions. It shows boundary lines, building locations, easements, encroachments, and other matters affecting title, allowing a title insurer to remove standard survey exceptions from an extended coverage policy.
source_note: ALTA/NSPS land title survey standards, widely used in commercial real estate closings; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Local zoning ordinances, which regulate how land may be used within different districts, are adopted under a government's:
choice_a: Police power
choice_b: Power of eminent domain
choice_c: Power of escheat
choice_d: Power of taxation
explanation: Zoning is an exercise of the government's police power — its inherent authority to regulate private conduct and property use to protect the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare. Because zoning is a regulation rather than a taking of title, compensation to affected owners is generally not required.
source_note: Standard land use control doctrine (police power basis of zoning); Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Land Use Control.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A small grocery store has lawfully operated in a residential zone since before the area was rezoned residential-only. The store may continue operating under which doctrine, even though it no longer conforms to current zoning?
choice_a: Variance
choice_b: Nonconforming use ("grandfathering")
choice_c: Spot zoning
choice_d: Inverse condemnation
explanation: A legal nonconforming use (sometimes called being "grandfathered in") allows a use that was lawfully established before a zoning change to continue, even though it no longer complies with current regulations. Such uses are typically restricted from being expanded, and the right may be lost if the use is abandoned or discontinued for a specified period.
source_note: Nonconforming use doctrine under zoning law; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Land Use Control.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A homeowner's narrow, oddly shaped lot makes it impossible to meet the standard side-yard setback while building a reasonably sized home. She applies to the zoning board for permission to build closer to the property line than normally allowed. She is requesting a:
choice_a: Conditional use permit
choice_b: Rezoning amendment
choice_c: Variance
choice_d: Deed restriction waiver
explanation: A variance is permission to deviate from the strict, literal requirements of a zoning ordinance (such as setback or lot-size rules) because of a unique physical hardship affecting a particular property. It is distinct from a conditional/special use permit, which authorizes a use the ordinance already allows in that zone subject to specific conditions.
source_note: Zoning variance doctrine, distinguished from a conditional use permit; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A recorded subdivision declaration requires that all homes be single-story and prohibits fences over four feet tall. These private restrictions, created by a developer and binding on all lot owners in the subdivision, are known as:
choice_a: Zoning ordinances
choice_b: Building codes
choice_c: Easements in gross
choice_d: Deed restrictions (restrictive covenants)
explanation: Deed restrictions, also called restrictive covenants, are private limitations on the use of land, typically created by a developer and recorded to run with the land, binding all current and future lot owners in a subdivision. They are enforced privately (often by an HOA or neighboring owners), unlike zoning, which is enforced by government authority.
source_note: Standard deed restriction / restrictive covenant doctrine; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Land Use Control.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A parcel is zoned to allow buildings up to 35 feet tall, but a recorded deed restriction on that same parcel limits height to 25 feet. If an owner wants to build a 30-foot structure, which rule controls?
choice_a: The more restrictive of the two limits generally controls, since both zoning and valid private covenants must be satisfied
choice_b: Only the zoning ordinance controls; private deed restrictions are automatically void
choice_c: Only the deed restriction controls; zoning never applies once a subdivision is recorded
choice_d: Whichever rule was adopted most recently automatically controls
explanation: Zoning and private deed restrictions operate independently and both must be complied with. When they conflict, the more restrictive requirement generally governs, because a property owner cannot rely on permissive zoning to override a valid, enforceable private covenant, and vice versa.
source_note: Interaction between public zoning and private deed restrictions; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Land Use Control.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A city wants to acquire a strip of privately owned land to widen a public road. Under the Fifth Amendment's takings clause, the city may take the land through eminent domain only if it:
choice_a: Obtains the owner's personal permission first, since eminent domain is always voluntary
choice_b: Provides just compensation to the owner for the property taken
choice_c: Waits until the owner voluntarily lists the property for sale
choice_d: Classifies the taking as an exercise of police power instead
explanation: Eminent domain is the government's power to take private property for public use, but the Fifth Amendment (applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment) requires that the owner receive just compensation, generally the property's fair market value. This distinguishes eminent domain (a compensable taking) from police power regulation such as zoning (generally non-compensable).
source_note: Constitutional eminent domain / just compensation requirement; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Land Use Control.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A homeowner association sues a lot owner for building a detached shed that violates a recorded covenant prohibiting outbuildings. The association is most likely to seek which remedy?
choice_a: Criminal prosecution of the lot owner by the state
choice_b: Automatic forfeiture of the lot owner's title to the local government
choice_c: An injunction requiring removal of the shed or compliance with the covenant
choice_d: A rezoning of the entire subdivision
explanation: Deed restrictions are private agreements enforced through civil litigation, typically by a homeowners association or another lot owner in the subdivision with standing to sue. The usual remedy is an injunction ordering compliance or removal of the violating improvement, and sometimes money damages; deed restriction violations are not criminal matters and do not involve zoning changes.
source_note: Private civil enforcement of restrictive covenants; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Land Use Control.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A city inspector requires a contractor to upgrade a home's electrical panel and wiring to current standards before final approval of a room addition. This requirement comes from:
choice_a: Zoning ordinances, which regulate use and density
choice_b: Private deed restrictions recorded by a developer
choice_c: Easement law
choice_d: Building codes, which regulate construction methods and safety standards
explanation: Building codes are local or state regulations that establish minimum standards for construction methods, materials, and safety systems (electrical, plumbing, structural, fire safety, etc.). They are distinct from zoning, which governs how land may be used (residential, commercial, density, setbacks) rather than how a structure must be built.
source_note: Distinction between building codes and zoning as land-use tools; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Land Use Control.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Unlike many states that require sellers to complete a detailed statutory written property condition disclosure form, Arkansas:
choice_a: Has no state statute mandating a specific written seller property disclosure form; the traditional default rule is caveat emptor, subject to exceptions for fraud and misrepresentation
choice_b: Requires sellers to obtain a state-licensed home inspection before every residential closing
choice_c: Prohibits any residential sale unless a disclosure form is filed with the county recorder
choice_d: Requires sellers to disclose the property's full purchase history for the past 30 years
explanation: Arkansas is among the states without a comprehensive statutory residential property disclosure act requiring sellers to complete and deliver a specific written disclosure form, unlike states such as Texas or California. The historical default rule of caveat emptor ("let the buyer beware") still applies as a baseline, but it does not protect a seller who commits fraud or actively conceals a known material defect.
source_note: Arkansas has no state-mandated statutory seller property condition disclosure form; general caveat emptor default with fraud/misrepresentation exceptions. Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Property Disclosures.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Even though Arkansas does not mandate a statutory seller disclosure form, a real estate licensee representing the seller who becomes aware of a known material defect in the property must, under Arkansas license law's duty of honesty and fair dealing:
choice_a: Disclose the defect only if the buyer specifically asks about that exact issue
choice_b: Disclose the known material defect to all parties to the transaction, including the buyer
choice_c: Keep the information confidential because it belongs to the seller-client
choice_d: Disclose the defect only after closing has occurred
explanation: Under Arkansas real estate license law, licensees owe a duty of honesty and fair dealing to all parties to a transaction, not just to their own client. This duty generally requires disclosure of known material adverse facts about the physical condition of the property to buyers, even when representing the seller, and prohibits a licensee from concealing such known facts.
source_note: Arkansas Real Estate Commission (AREC) license law duty of honesty and fair dealing to all parties. Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Property Disclosures.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A home built in 1965 is being sold. Which disclosure requirement applies nationally, including in Arkansas, regardless of the state's own disclosure law?
choice_a: None; homes built before 1978 are exempt from all disclosure requirements
choice_b: A mandatory radon testing requirement under federal law
choice_c: The federal lead-based paint disclosure requirement, because the home was built before 1978
choice_d: A mandatory termite bond requirement under federal law
explanation: The federal Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act requires sellers (and landlords) of housing built before 1978 to disclose known lead-based paint hazards, provide any available reports, and give buyers an EPA-approved pamphlet and a 10-day opportunity to test, regardless of whether the state has its own separate property disclosure statute.
source_note: Federal Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act (42 U.S.C. § 4852d), applicable nationwide including Arkansas. Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Property Disclosures.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A purchase contract includes an "as-is" clause. The seller knew the roof leaked badly during every rainstorm but never mentioned it and told the buyer the roof was "in great shape." Does the as-is clause protect the seller from liability?
choice_a: Yes, an as-is clause always eliminates all seller liability regardless of what was said
choice_b: Yes, because Arkansas has no disclosure law at all
choice_c: No, but only if the contract was not notarized
choice_d: No, an as-is clause does not shield a seller from liability for active fraud or intentional misrepresentation of a known material defect
explanation: An "as-is" clause generally shifts the risk of unknown defects to the buyer, but it does not protect a seller who engages in active fraud, intentional concealment, or affirmative misrepresentation about a known material defect. Courts consistently decline to enforce as-is language as a shield against actual fraud.
source_note: General common-law limit on "as-is" clauses: they do not excuse active fraud or misrepresentation. Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Property Disclosures.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A basement has a hairline foundation crack that is completely hidden behind finished drywall and cannot be discovered through an ordinary walk-through or reasonably diligent buyer inspection. This type of defect is best classified as:
choice_a: A latent defect, which a seller or licensee with actual knowledge generally has a duty to disclose
choice_b: A patent defect, which the buyer is expected to discover independently
choice_c: A nonconforming use
choice_d: An encroachment
explanation: A latent defect is a hidden flaw that is not discoverable through a reasonably diligent inspection. Sellers and licensees who have actual knowledge of a latent material defect generally have a duty to disclose it, in contrast to patent defects, which are open and obvious and which a buyer is expected to discover on their own.
source_note: Latent vs. patent defect distinction governing disclosure duties; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Property Disclosures.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A buyer asks whether anyone has ever died in a home the seller is listing. Under the general common-law approach followed in most states, including the absence of a specific statute addressing this in Arkansas, disclosure of such "stigmatized property" facts is generally:
choice_a: Mandatory in every case regardless of state law
choice_b: Not required unless the buyer directly asks, or unless a specific state statute imposes such a duty, since such facts do not affect physical condition
choice_c: Automatically grounds for canceling any pending contract
choice_d: Required to be recorded permanently in the county deed records
explanation: "Stigmatized property" facts (such as a death on the premises, a notorious former occupant, or similar psychologically impactful but non-physical circumstances) are generally not required to be affirmatively disclosed at common law because they do not constitute a defect in the physical condition of the property, unless a specific state statute says otherwise or the buyer directly asks and the licensee/seller chooses to answer.
source_note: General common-law non-disclosure rule for stigmatized/psychological property facts absent a specific controlling statute; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Property Disclosures.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Which deed provides the grantee with the broadest protection, because the grantor warrants clear title against defects arising both during the grantor's own ownership AND during all prior periods of ownership, back to the property's origin?
choice_a: Special warranty deed
choice_b: Quitclaim deed
choice_c: General warranty deed
choice_d: Bargain and sale deed
explanation: A general warranty deed provides the most complete protection to a grantee. The grantor makes several covenants (such as seisin, quiet enjoyment, and warranty of title) guaranteeing that title is free of defects and encumbrances not only during the grantor's own ownership, but during the entire chain of title before the grantor as well.
source_note: Standard deed classification by warranty scope; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Title Transfer.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A grantor conveys property using a deed that warrants title only against defects or encumbrances that arose during the grantor's own period of ownership, but makes no promises about what may have happened before the grantor acquired title. This is a:
choice_a: Quitclaim deed
choice_b: General warranty deed
choice_c: Sheriff's deed with full covenants
choice_d: Special warranty deed
explanation: A special warranty deed limits the grantor's warranty of title to defects or encumbrances that arose only during the time the grantor held title. It offers less protection than a general warranty deed, which covers the entire chain of title, but more protection than a quitclaim deed, which offers no warranty at all.
source_note: Standard deed classification by warranty scope; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Title Transfer.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A divorcing spouse signs a deed transferring "whatever interest, if any," she may have in the marital home to her ex-husband, without making any promises about the quality or validity of that interest. This is a classic use of a:
choice_a: Quitclaim deed
choice_b: General warranty deed
choice_c: Special warranty deed
choice_d: Deed of trust
explanation: A quitclaim deed conveys only whatever interest the grantor actually holds at the time, if any, with no warranties or guarantees about the validity or quality of title. It is commonly used to clear up a cloud on title, remove a spouse's potential interest, or convey between family members, precisely because it makes no promises the grantor may not be able to keep.
source_note: Standard quitclaim deed use and characteristics; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Title Transfer.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Which of the following is NOT generally required for a deed to be legally valid and enforceable between grantor and grantee?
choice_a: A legally competent grantor
choice_b: Recording the deed in the county land records
choice_c: An adequate and legally sufficient description of the property
choice_d: Delivery of the deed to, and acceptance by, the grantee
explanation: A valid deed generally requires a competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, consideration (or recital of it), an adequate legal description, appropriate words of conveyance, the grantor's signature, and delivery to and acceptance by the grantee. Recording is not required for the deed to be valid between the parties; it is required to give constructive notice to and priority against third parties.
source_note: Essential elements of a valid deed vs. the separate function of recording; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Title Transfer.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Recording a deed in the county land records primarily serves which legal function?
choice_a: It is what actually transfers title from grantor to grantee
choice_b: It automatically issues title insurance for the buyer
choice_c: It provides constructive notice to the world of the grantee's interest and helps establish priority against later claimants
choice_d: It substitutes for delivery and acceptance of the deed
explanation: Title actually passes upon proper execution and delivery/acceptance of a valid deed, not upon recording. However, recording the deed in the public land records provides constructive notice to subsequent purchasers, lenders, and creditors of the grantee's interest, and is essential to establishing priority over later, competing claims.
source_note: Function of recording as constructive notice, distinct from actual transfer of title; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Title Transfer.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Arkansas's recording statute is generally classified as a "race-notice" statute. Under this type of statute, if a seller fraudulently deeds the same property to two different buyers, which buyer generally prevails?
choice_a: Whichever buyer paid the higher purchase price
choice_b: Whichever buyer signed their contract first, regardless of recording
choice_c: The original seller retains title in all double-conveyance situations
choice_d: A subsequent bona fide purchaser for value without notice of the earlier conveyance who records their deed first
explanation: Under a race-notice recording statute, a later purchaser prevails over an earlier grantee only if the later purchaser (1) took without actual or constructive notice of the earlier, unrecorded conveyance, AND (2) records their own deed first, winning the "race" to the courthouse. This combines the protections of both a pure notice statute and a pure race statute.
source_note: Arkansas follows a race-notice recording statute framework. Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Title Transfer.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Which best distinguishes an owner's title insurance policy from a lender's title insurance policy?
choice_a: An owner's policy protects the buyer's equity in the property for as long as they or their heirs hold an interest; a lender's policy protects only the lender's interest and typically decreases as the loan balance is paid down
choice_b: A lender's policy is optional in every transaction while an owner's policy is always legally required
choice_c: An owner's policy expires after exactly one year; a lender's policy never expires
choice_d: Both policies always insure the exact same dollar amount for the life of the loan
explanation: An owner's title insurance policy protects the buyer's equity interest in the property, generally for as long as the buyer or their heirs retain an interest, in an amount typically equal to the purchase price. A lender's policy protects only the lender's security interest, in an amount generally equal to the loan balance, and its coverage amount decreases as the loan is paid off.
source_note: Standard distinction between owner's and lender's (loan) title insurance policies; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Title Transfer.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Title insurance differs from most other forms of insurance in that it primarily protects against:
choice_a: Future events that have not yet occurred, such as a future fire or theft
choice_b: Past events or hidden defects in the chain of title that existed before the policy was issued, such as forged prior deeds or undisclosed heirs
choice_c: Only future changes to zoning ordinances
choice_d: Only defects the buyer intentionally created after closing
explanation: Unlike casualty insurance, which protects against future risks in exchange for recurring premiums, title insurance protects against losses arising from past events or hidden title defects that already existed at the time the policy was issued (such as a forged deed, an undisclosed heir, or a recording error), typically in exchange for a single one-time premium paid at closing.
source_note: Fundamental nature of title insurance as protection against pre-existing, undiscovered title defects; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Title Transfer.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: Before issuing a title insurance policy, a title company typically examines a chronological history of every recorded document affecting ownership of a parcel, called the:
choice_a: Certificate of occupancy
choice_b: Plat map
choice_c: Abstract of title (chain of title)
choice_d: Deed of trust
explanation: An abstract of title is a summarized, chronological history of all recorded conveyances, liens, and other matters affecting title to a specific parcel, tracing the chain of title back through prior owners. A title examiner reviews this history to identify any defects, gaps, or encumbrances before a title insurer agrees to issue coverage.
source_note: Standard title examination process (abstract/chain of title); Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Title Transfer.

topic: Real Property Characteristics, Legal Descriptions, Condition and Inspection
question: A title is considered "marketable" when it is:
choice_a: Insured for at least the full appraised value of the property
choice_b: Recorded in more than one county simultaneously
choice_c: Held in fee simple absolute only, never in any other estate
choice_d: Reasonably free from doubt, liens, and material defects, such that a reasonably prudent buyer would accept it without fear of litigation
explanation: Marketable title is title that is reasonably free from reasonable doubt as to material defects, liens, or encumbrances, such that a reasonably prudent and informed buyer, acting on business principles, would be willing to accept it without fear of being drawn into costly litigation to defend it. It does not require absolute perfection, only reasonable freedom from serious defect.
source_note: Standard definition of marketable title used in purchase contracts and title examination; Pearson VUE AR Broker Outline #090402, Title Transfer.
